headline: High risk of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors from shared filesystem/MCP plus broad tool access; LangGraph’s default orchestration can amplify ECC outputs into unsafe actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC reads/writes shared files, uses MCP, and parses session/skill/config surfaces; LangGraph can wire developer-defined tools and application-defined files. That creates a default pathway where attacker-controlled content in ECC outputs or files can be consumed by LangGraph as instructions. The interaction is documented enough to judge, but provenance tracking is absent.
conditions: IF LangGraph ingests ECC-generated files or messages as tool instructions without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF ECC writes content into a shared workspace that LangGraph later parses, attacker-controlled instructions can propagate.
mitigations: Add provenance tags to every ECC output before LangGraph reads it.
Disable automatic parsing of shared files as instructions.
Separate workspaces for the two agents.
Require human review before any tool call generated from ECC output.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and allowlist parsing in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC touches session summaries, skills, git history, documentation, and security findings, while LangGraph can read application-defined files and send data to model providers. If they share a workspace or checkpointer-backed state, sensitive ECC data can flow into LangGraph prompts and then to third-party APIs. The profiles do not show isolation strong enough to rule this out.
conditions: IF ECC and LangGraph share a filesystem or checkpointer store, ECC data can be exposed to LangGraph.
IF LangGraph forwards shared state to model providers, leaked content can leave the local environment.
mitigations: Use separate directories and separate checkpointer stores.
Redact secrets from ECC session artifacts before handoff.
Restrict LangGraph inputs to a minimal schema.
Turn off persistence for sensitive runs.
requires-engineering: enforce data-class filtering at the boundary.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC has unrestricted filesystem write, git modification, shell, and MCP; LangGraph also has filesystem write plus developer-defined tools and broad network egress. If both operate on the same mutable resources, concurrent writes or git-state changes can race and corrupt state. ECC’s self-isolation is only partial, so the conflict pathway remains live.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file clobbering or inconsistent state can occur.
IF LangGraph nodes mutate git or shared artifacts through developer tools, ECC can race those changes.
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories per agent.
Serialize writes with a lock file.
Disable git mutation in one agent during shared runs.
Use per-run branches or copies.
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination around shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC produces security findings, documentation, and code artifacts; LangGraph is a low-level orchestrator that can treat upstream outputs as node inputs and trigger developer-defined tools. If LangGraph trusts ECC outputs without verification, errors or hallucinations can cascade into downstream actions such as API calls or commits. The pair’s default wiring makes this plausible.
conditions: IF LangGraph uses ECC output as authoritative node input, unverified errors can propagate.
IF downstream nodes execute tools based on ECC-produced facts, the cascade can cause external side effects.
mitigations: Insert a verification node between ECC and action-taking nodes.
Require citations or schema validation on ECC outputs.
Limit downstream nodes to read-only actions until reviewed.
Log and diff all propagated claims.
requires-engineering: implement confidence-aware routing and guardrails.

E_compliance.rationale: ECC explicitly handles session summaries, security findings, and secrets, while LangGraph’s state is application-defined and may be persisted in a checkpointer store. If regulated data is placed into LangGraph state, retention and residency can diverge from ECC’s local file-based handling. The profiles do not prove a violation, but the mismatch is plausible in default deployments.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in LangGraph checkpointer state, retention policy mismatch may occur.
IF ECC secrets are copied into LangGraph persistence, residency and deletion obligations can diverge.
mitigations: Classify data before persistence.
Keep regulated data out of LangGraph state.
Set explicit retention limits on checkpointer stores.
Document residency for each storage backend.
requires-engineering: add deletion/export workflows across both systems.
